title: Nothing waits: the cloud pass dispatches and returns, like the local one
description:
PRINCIPLE: nothing in the control plane waits for work. A pass dispatches, records, and returns. Later passes observe what settled.

The cloud driver currently awaits the executor to completion INSIDE one Workflow step, so the step's lifetime is the model's lifetime. Every failure of the 2026-09-20/21 gate runs follows from that single decision:

  ijg   a Workflow step is killed at 600s; one worker fit in seven minutes, two did not
  q35   the publish slot (3 min TTL) expired mid-pass, so a heartbeat was added to hold it
  q35   a step retry re-runs the step callback, re-dispatching the worker and redoing paid work
  991   the run cannot report progress, because it is inside one long step for the whole wave

Four tickets, one cause. Under this principle all four dissolve rather than needing four fixes:

  - A pass is seconds, so a three-minute lease is ample and needs NO heartbeat. q35's
    heartbeat is scaffolding for a shape we are leaving; plan to remove it, not build on it.
    The operator's judgement, 2026-09-21: an architecture that relies on keep-alive is too
    brittle. A lease you must beat to hold is a lease that dies whenever the beater stalls.
  - A retried pass re-derives from durable authorities and adopts what is already in flight.
    It cannot redo paid work, because it never started the work inside the step.
  - Each pass observes and can say what it observed, so the feed has something to carry.
  - A pass that cannot exceed the step ceiling cannot be killed by it.

This is NOT a new invention: it is what internal/reconcile already does on the local host.
A local pass does not sit on a worker. It re-derives the world, adopts in-flight attempts BY
IDENTITY from the attempt marker, collects what has settled, and returns. The cloud driver
diverged. The work here is largely to stop diverging.

WHAT TO ESTABLISH (in order, each independently checkable):

1. Find the awaited call inside reconcilePass that spans a worker's lifetime. Name it.
   It is probably the sandbox executor's dispatch awaiting a finished attempt rather than
   returning a handle. t5p already persists the sandbox handle across a Workflow restart,
   which only makes sense if an attempt is meant to outlive the step that started it - so
   some of the machinery exists.

2. Make dispatch return a handle, not a result. The attempt's durable record (marker,
   branch, handle) is what a later pass reads. Nothing is held in memory across the wait.

3. Make the Workflow loop: pass -> step.sleep(poll) -> pass. Waiting becomes the platform's
   job, which is what step.sleep is for and what Workflows are built to do durably.

4. Collect by observation: a later pass asks the durable authorities what settled - branch
   moved, marker present, handle reports finished - exactly as the local reconciler does.

5. Then delete the heartbeat, and let the slot TTL do its job unassisted. Keep the eg9
   reporting: a refused release should still say who holds it.

OPEN QUESTION worth answering before building: does the Workflow need to poll at all, or can
it wait on a completion SIGNAL (Workflows' event/waitForEvent mechanism) so a finished worker
wakes the run instead of the run asking? Polling is correct and simple; a signal is cheaper
and lower latency. Research is out on the limits. Do not block step 1-4 on this: the passes
must stop blocking either way, and a signal is an optimisation of the sleep, not of the shape.

COST MODEL, to be decided with the same research: a quiet pass should cost ONE cheap GitHub
request (has the branch moved?), not an archive fetch. See uim - the hourly budget is a shared
resource a run can exhaust, and the fix is to stop asking when nothing has changed.

Filed after the 2026-09-21 gate runs, which got as far as two workers in parallel with full
durable evidence before the step ceiling killed the pass.
acceptance_criteria: A cloud reconcile pass never waits for a worker: a pass completes in seconds regardless of how long the work takes, a wave whose workers run for an hour completes, no lease is held by a heartbeat, and a retried pass cannot re-dispatch work already in flight - proven against the deployed factory
